passage: Anirban, you're frowning about your goal today. Sit, and I'll tell you about mine. I am Dolma, and at eleven I hit the last point that won our volleyball game in Leh. I jumped up screaming. Then I saw Tenzin, who had wanted that last spike all season, standing with his arms folded, silent. He didn't come to the tea afterwards. I knew why. I walked over and said, "Your pass set that up, you know. I couldn't have hit it without you." He shrugged, but his shoulders came down. I didn't pretend I hadn't scored, either. I said, "The next one is yours, if you're ready." He smiled a little.

qa.q: Where did Dolma win the volleyball game?
qa.a: In a volleyball game in Leh.

qa.q: What was Tenzin probably feeling after Dolma's winning point?
qa.a: Envy or disappointment, since he had wanted that last spike all season and stood silent with his arms folded.

qa.q: What could Anirban do if a teammate sulks after Anirban's goal?
qa.a: Credit the teammate's pass, include him, and still be honest about scoring. 🙂

qa.q: Why might Dolma have gone over to Tenzin instead of only celebrating?
qa.a: Dolma knew why Tenzin was upset and wanted him to feel his part mattered, so Dolma credited his pass without pretending not to have scored.

grounding: An elder recalls scoring the winning point while a teammate who wanted that chance went quiet; the narrator credited his pass and included him without hiding their own goal.

passage:
Saturday
We WON the basketball match! I scored the last basket with two seconds left. Everyone screamed. Nandini Ma'am hugged the whole team.
But Rohit went quiet. He sat on the bench, untying and retying his shoes. He'd wanted that last shot. He'd practised all week.
I felt a bit awkward. Then I remembered: he passed me the ball. Without that pass, there was no basket.
So I went over. "Rohit, that pass was perfect. You set it up."
He looked up. "Really?"
"Really. Want to practise free throws together tomorrow?"
He nodded. I'm still really happy I scored. But it was both of us.
Mridul

qa.q: How many seconds were left when Mridul scored?
How did Mridul feel when Rohit went quiet?
qa.a: Mridul felt awkward, still happy about scoring but uneasy, knowing Rohit had wanted that last shot after practising all week.

qa.q: What did Mridul do that was wise?
qa.a: Mridul credited Rohit's pass and invited him to practise, without pretending the basket didn't matter.

qa.q: How might Rohit feel after Mridul praised the pass?
qa.a: Rohit would likely feel seen and included, and less left out of the win.

grounding: Mridul scores the winning basket and a teammate goes quiet; Mridul credits his pass and includes him without downplaying the win completely.

passage:
At the village football match, Asif scored the winning goal in the last minute. The crowd by the banyan tree cheered wildly.
But Kunal, who had been clapping a second ago, suddenly went silent. He walked to the edge of the field and kicked at the grass. Asif knew Kunal had been dreaming of that winning goal all season.
Asif went over. "Kunal, I only scored because of your cross. It was brilliant."
Kunal shrugged. "You still scored."
"Yes, and I'm happy about it. But it was your ball. Next match, you take the penalty if we get one."
Kunal looked up and smiled a little.

qa.q: How did Asif feel when he saw Kunal kicking at the grass?
qa.a: Asif felt happy about his goal but also sympathetic and a little uneasy, knowing Kunal had dreamed of that goal all season.

qa.q: How did Asif handle Kunal's sulking?
qa.a: He credited Kunal's cross and offered him the next penalty, while still being happy about his own goal.

qa.q: How might Kunal feel after Asif's offer?
qa.a: Kunal seemed to feel better and included, smiling a little.

grounding: A boy scores the winning goal and a teammate sulks; he credits the teammate's cross and includes him, without downplaying himself entirely.
